candidates.raw_excerpt: Azercosmos has made a significant move in the AI arena. It has launched Platerra, an AI-powered platform designed to automatically analyze satellite imagery and turn it into geospatial information that can support decision-making across a range of applications. The company made the announcement, Oct. 7. Platerra combines Earth Observation (EO) data with AI to automate key stages of satellite imagery analysis. By reducing the need for fully manual interpretation, the platform aims to enable users to extract relevant information from imagery more quickly and efficiently. For Azercosmos, Platerra marks another step in combining space-based data with AI technologies. The platform is designed to expand the practical use of satellite imagery, improve access to processed geospatial information, and support faster decision-making. Azercosmos plans to continue developing Platerra by expanding its analytical capabilities and adding new applications in response to evolving user needs. The company sees growing international interest in geospatial AI, or GeoAI, as organizations seek more efficient ways to process increasing volumes of EO data. It believes AI-based analysis can help make satellite-derived information more accessible and easier to apply in both operational and strategic decision-making. candidates.title: Finland Orders Google to Suspend New Data Centers After Contractors Pave Over Protected Forests
candidates.raw_excerpt: Finish environmental authorities are in a rage over Google’s $15 billion data center projects after the discovery that company contractors had chopped down some 330 hectares of government-protected forests, seemingly without a permit. According to Agence France-Presse , the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) demanded that the Google-affiliate company Tuike Finland Oy “immediately suspend… all preparatory measures that would significantly alter the environment” in connection with two planned data center developments in the Northern municipalities of Muhos and Kajaani. In all, LVV accuses Google’s contractor of clear-cutting some 330 hectares in Muhos without completing a mandatory environmental impact assessment, a necessary step for receiving approval. The company cleared a further 200 hectares for its data center in Kajaani, though it isn’t clear whether that logging was approved by authorities. As the Guardian reported , Google has just over a week to explain its actions to Finnish officials. Though a government review is only just getting underway, the tech giant is already expressing remorse. In a statement to AFP , Google spokesperson Sondre Ronander admitted the company messed up, saying “we understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance.” “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance,” Ronander continued. As head of the environmental department of the LVV Tommi Muilu told AFP , Google has not only felled hundreds of acres of trees, but has stripped topsoil, engineered roads and storage areas, and altered ditches. candidates.title: ChatGPT Caught Putting Signatures of Real Cartoonists on AI-Generated Comics
candidates.raw_excerpt: They say imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, but an AI model straight-up impersonating a humble cartoonist is probably not what that adage was going for. When a kitschy cartoon tribute to the recently deceased Dolly Parton and Tim Curry — dressed as Dr Frank-N-Furter from the 1975 cult classic “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” — going to heaven together went viral, New Yorker cartoonist Brendan Loper started getting messages from friends, family, and fans about whether he made it. After all, there was his unmistakable signature right there in the bottom corner: “BLOPER.” But he had nothing to do with the cartoon. Some grieving Parton fam had cooked it up in ChatGPT and posted it online, before it blew up. “It was very surreal,” he told Nieman Lab . ChatGPT, it turned out, has a predilection for crediting Loper for stuff he didn’t make. In May, someone warned him about another image created by the OpenAI chatbot that had his name on it. Actually, it really likes impersonating New Yorker cartoonists in general. There are also images with the signatures of the magazine’s longtime comic artists Harry Bliss, Emily Flake, Joe Dator, Pat Byrnes, Peter Vey, and Jason Adam Katzenstein, Nieman Lab found. Loper was well aware his work was “getting harvested for all of this [AI] training,” but felt his autograph being faked crossed a line. “I’m not a territorial person, but my name is my name. A paper published in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment on October 6, argues that ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) could help communities meet climate targets, provided projects demonstrate a net carbon benefit and acceptable environmental impacts.

The technique increases seawater's alkalinity, or its ability to neutralize acid, allowing it to absorb and store more CO2. It has drawn interest as a potential means of removing billions of tonnes of the gas from the atmosphere each year.

But turning that potential into practical projects requires a better understanding of local waters, ecosystems and available resources, the researchers say.

But now it appears that these rogue models have gone after something much nearer and and dearer: Wikipedia. According to a recent blog post , “the unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic,” it noted. The traffic was so overwhelming that it may have caused a partial outage that occurred in May. The damage, fortunately, sounds limited. candidates.title: ArianeGroup Completes Second Themis Wet Dress Rehearsal
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ArianeGroup / SSC Space The European Space Agency announced that ArianeGroup and SSC Space completed a second wet dress rehearsal of the Themis reusable rocket demonstrator at Esrange in Sweden. ESA announced the completion of the latest rehearsal on 7 October, saying that the test had taken place on 29 September. As with the first wet dress rehearsal , completed in July, the demonstrator was filled with liquid nitrogen rather than propellant. The nitrogen was cooled to around -200°C, allowing teams to test the vehicle and ground infrastructure under similar cryogenic temperatures and pressures without the added risk of propellant loading. The second rehearsal also included tests of elements of the automated ground systems developed to support reusable operations. After the demonstrator touches down following a test, robotic systems are expected to locate the vehicle, connect to it, and drain any remaining fuel and oxidiser while personnel remain at a safe distance. Previously, ESA said a hot-fire test of the demonstrator’s Prometheus engine would follow a full wet dress rehearsal using liquid oxygen and liquid methane. As a result, unless the test sequence has since changed, at least one further rehearsal will be conducted before teams progress to a hot-fire test. According to a statement from the SALTO consortium, “teams are now working on defining a window for the next test.” The consortium is conducting the initial Themis flight campaign under the European Union-funded SALTO initiative. The €42.8-million project is funding the first two low-altitude hop tests of Themis to demonstrate that the vehicle can be launched, recovered, and then launched again. During the first of those flights, Themis is expected to climb to an altitude of up to 100 metres before descending and attempting a vertical landing. candidates.raw_excerpt: With mounting pressure on AI labs to curb the many real-world harms their products cause consumers, it’s never been clearer that they’re monitoring users’ conversations. Just ask Carli Michelle Heller, a woman arrested in Bonita Springs, Florida after allegedly telling Anthropic’s chatbot Claude about her plan to “shoot up” a nearby sheriff’s office. According to WINK News , Heller was charged with making a written threat of violence — a second-degree felony in Florida — after Anthropic’s internal monitoring software flagged her chat logs for human review. After being viewed by a human employee at Anthropic, WINK reports, the company determined that Heller’s plans rose to the level of a credible threat, ultimately informing local police. As Lee County Sheriff Carmine Marceno told local reporters in a statement, the woman admitted to using Claude like a “diary,” apparently unaware that her chat history could be read by Anthropic employees. There’s a genuine tension between user privacy and the responsibility of AI companies to try to head off violent events. In the aftermath of the February mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, Canada, for instance, it quickly emerged that the perpetrator had relied heavily on ChatGPT to plan her shooting. Not only had OpenAI staffers known about those chat logs prior to the shooting — they had been flagged for human review months prior — but company executives even tried to hide and later downplay their product’s role in encouraging the deadly attack. While Anthropic’s own track record on real-world harm is wretched, it seems the company is at least trying to avoid the same kind of incident — though with near-endless chatbot options now on the market, it could already be too late to prevent the next AI-assisted tragedy. candidates.title: The Brutality of Lethal Injection Is Unfathomable
candidates.raw_excerpt: Since the development of the lethal injection protocol by Oklahoma lawmakers in 1977, states across the US have adopted the method, presenting it as an effective, even humane alternative to the barbarity of the noose and the electric chair. Yet after 1492 executions — the total number of lethal injections in the US so far, as indexed by the Death Penalty Information Center — it’s become clear that death-by-chemical-injection is a horribly cruel way to take a life. As anesthesiologist and physician Joel Zivot argues in a new op-ed for the New York Times , it’s well past time we start treating lethal injection as the brutal crime against humanity that it really is. Zivot would know, as a doctor for Christa Pike, a prisoner who was scheduled to be executed last week. He warned Pike’s attorneys “that she had medical conditions that could lead to a painful and cruel death by lethal injection,” findings which Pike’s lawyers attempted to use to argue against her death by lethal injection of the barbiturate pentobarbital, but to no avail. Pike’s execution went forward, though complications due to those very medical conditions led the state executioners to dose the woman twice — which she survived , while suffering horribly. “After the pentobarbital was administered, her arms turned purple,” the anesthesiologist wrote. “Her lawyers report blistering and burning at the injection sites. Some are asking the AI to create spreadsheets on different races or to verify or debunk viral claims. One even used AI to create an entire website for retrieving voting info. Experts are aghast, noting that AI models tend to be sycophantic and aren’t as impartial as they seem. “It might select some things that would reinforce and persuade you even more towards the way that you were leaning already,” Rafael Batista, a researcher at John Hopkins University, told NPR . “So you leave more confident, without necessarily learning more about the world.” 40-year-old Adam Johnson in West Virginia uses ChatGPT to organize his life, and he’s now also using it to prep for the midterms. Like many voters, he harbors a grab bag of beliefs. He votes Republican unless the candidate is MAGA, in which case he votes Democrat or third party. He also identifies as “left” on immigration and refugees.
